pairs.question: Cur haec igitur adhuc parum profecerunt?
pairs.answer: Quia non putat se sustinere causas posse multorum, si tibi, cui iustius videtur irasci posse, concesserit.
pairs.derivation: Cicero poses his own question (why Caesar's clement nature has so far helped little) and answers it himself with quia. Answer ends at the first full stop (concesserit); what follows is the next imagined objection ('Quae est igitur...spes ab irato?').

pairs.question: Quae est igitur spes ab irato?
pairs.answer: Eodem e fonte se hausturum intelligit laudes suas, e quo sit leviter aspersus.
pairs.derivation: Caecina is imagined to ask the question (framed by 'inquies', which is dropped as a speech tag interpolated into the quotation; the two quoted fragments 'Quae est igitur,' and 'spes ab irato?' are the speaker's contiguous words minus the tag). Cicero answers directly. Answer runs to the first full stop (aspersus); what follows is a new point ('Postremo homo valde est acutus...').

pairs.question: Quo igitur haec spectant?
pairs.answer: Rerum hoc natura et civilium temporum non patietur, nec manens nec mutata ratio feret, primum ut non in causa pari eadem sit et condicio et fortuna omnium, deinde ut in eam civitatem boni viri et boni cives nulla ignominia notati non reverbantur, in quam tot nefariorum scelerum condemnati reverterunt.
pairs.derivation: Cicero asks to what his examples of Caesar's clemency point, then answers in his own voice. Answer ends at the first full stop (reverterunt); what follows ('Habes augurium meum...') turns to summing up. Editorial brackets none present.
